title: API returning intermittent 504s under heavy load
problem: The Payments team saw authorization requests time out once traffic exceeded roughly 800 requests/sec after adding a fraud check.
symptoms: Gateway 504s reached 8%; p95 was 5.0s while application CPU stayed below 40%. HikariCP showed 40 active connections, zero idle, and acquire p95 of 4.6s; logs reported connection acquisition timed out.
root_cause: A Spring transaction acquired a PostgreSQL connection before a remote fraud call and held it for up to 2s. The 40-connection pool saturated despite low database CPU.

attempted_solutions.solution: Raised the gateway timeout from 5s to 30s.
attempted_solutions.result: Visible 504s fell temporarily, but queued requests and connection waits grew; the change concealed exhaustion.

attempted_solutions.solution: Increased each pod pool from 40 to 80.
attempted_solutions.result: Eight pods exceeded the database connection budget during rollout, introducing too many clients errors.

successful_solution: Moved the fraud request outside the database transaction, kept only ledger writes inside it, restored 40 connections per pod, and bounded request concurrency to the measured database budget.
outcome: Issue load-test attachment showed 504s falling from 8% to 0.2% at 1,000 requests/sec, p95 from 5.0s to 310ms, and connection acquire p95 below 20ms over a 45-minute run.
applicable_when: An API times out under concurrency with saturated connection pools, low database CPU, and transactions spanning network calls; applicable to checkout and other transactional services.

title: Checkout 504s caused by a slow payment provider
problem: The Commerce team saw intermittent checkout 504s at the evening sales peak even though order database queries remained fast.
symptoms: 504 rate reached 6%, checkout p95 hit the 5s gateway deadline, and traces spent 4.7s in the payment-provider span. Database pool utilization stayed below 35% and connection acquisition below 5ms.
root_cause: The external authorization provider degraded to 4-8s responses; the client had an 8s timeout and occupied request workers beyond the gateway deadline.

attempted_solutions.solution: Doubled the order database connection pool.
attempted_solutions.result: Latency did not change because requests were waiting on the provider, not PostgreSQL.

attempted_solutions.solution: Retried every provider timeout immediately.
attempted_solutions.result: Provider traffic rose 70% and worsened throttling; uncertain authorizations required reconciliation.

successful_solution: Set a 2s provider deadline and circuit breaker, reused a durable idempotency key, and returned a pending-payment state for uncertain authorizations that a reconciliation worker resolved.
outcome: PR canary report recorded gateway 504s falling from 6% to 0.3% and checkout p95 to 2.2s; 2.1% of payments remained pending, with 98% reconciled within two minutes.
applicable_when: 504s align with downstream spans while local pools and queries are healthy; useful for payments, shipping, and other external-service calls.

title: Profile API slows under traffic spikes despite available connections
problem: The Identity team saw profile search become unusable above 600 requests/sec as the tenant directory passed 12 million records.
symptoms: p95 increased from 240ms to 3.8s, with 1.5% gateway 504s. PostgreSQL CPU reached 92%; pool acquisition stayed below 15ms, and EXPLAIN showed sequential scans for tenant_id plus lower(email).
root_cause: The existing email index could not support the case-insensitive, tenant-scoped lookup, so each request scanned millions of rows.

attempted_solutions.solution: Increased API workers from 8 to 16.
attempted_solutions.result: Database CPU stayed saturated and query concurrency increased.

attempted_solutions.solution: Added an index on email alone.
attempted_solutions.result: The lower(email) predicate still prevented use of that index and tenant filtering remained expensive.

successful_solution: Created a concurrent composite expression index on (tenant_id, lower(email)), refreshed statistics, and confirmed the production query used an index scan.
outcome: Issue query plans and a one-hour replay showed p95 dropping from 3.8s to 180ms, database CPU to 48%, and 504s below 0.1%; bulk directory exports remained slow.
applicable_when: Latency rises with table size and database CPU, but connection acquisition is fast; relevant to tenant-scoped search in checkout and analytics.

title: Search 504s caused by expensive wildcard queries
problem: The Discovery team saw search timeouts during a product launch after enabling substring matching on SKU fields.
symptoms: Gateway 504s reached 4%; search p95 was 5.0s. OpenSearch search threads queued 1,200 tasks, node CPU hit 95%, and the slow log repeatedly contained leading-wildcard queries.
root_cause: Queries such as *adapter* expanded across high-cardinality keyword terms and consumed the search cluster CPU; the API itself was healthy.

attempted_solutions.solution: Added two API replicas.
attempted_solutions.result: Search-node utilization and timeouts did not improve because the bottleneck was downstream query execution.

successful_solution: Built an n-gram search field in a replacement index, switched substring queries to that field, capped query length, and rate-limited the expensive legacy path during reindexing.
outcome: PR benchmark showed p95 falling from 5.0s to 460ms and 504s to 0.2% at the same request rate; index storage increased 28%.
applicable_when: Timeouts coincide with search-engine CPU and wildcard slow logs rather than database pool waits; relevant to catalog and analytics search.

title: Redis outage turns cart reads into a database stampede
problem: The Commerce team lost the cart Redis primary during a failover rehearsal and overloaded PostgreSQL within 30 seconds.
symptoms: Redis connection errors reached 100% for 42s, database reads rose from 2,000 to 18,000/sec, and cart p95 increased from 90ms to 2.6s.
root_cause: Every cache miss fell back independently to the database, including thousands of simultaneous reads for the same promoted carts; Redis reconnects had no backoff.

attempted_solutions.solution: Increased the Redis client timeout from 100ms to 1s.
attempted_solutions.result: Requests waited longer on the failed primary and still flooded the database afterward.

successful_solution: Added per-key request coalescing, jittered reconnect backoff, a cache circuit breaker, and a strict concurrency cap on database fallback; returned retryable errors when the cap was full.
outcome: Issue failover replay kept database reads below 4,500/sec and cart p95 at 380ms; 0.8% of reads received retryable errors during the 40s outage.
applicable_when: Cache failure multiplies backend reads; transferable to user profiles and search metadata, with stale serving only where business semantics permit.

title: Report joins spill to disk after statistics drift
problem: The Insights team saw daily account reports grow from 12s to more than three minutes after a large backfill.
symptoms: EXPLAIN ANALYZE estimated 8,000 rows but processed 9 million, hash joins spilled 6GB to temporary files, and dashboard requests frequently exceeded the 60s deadline.
root_cause: Bulk ingestion changed tenant data distribution faster than automatic analyze ran, causing a poor join order and undersized hash estimates.

attempted_solutions.solution: Doubled report worker memory.
attempted_solutions.result: PostgreSQL still chose the same poor plan; application memory did not change database planning.

successful_solution: Ran targeted ANALYZE, increased statistics targets on skewed tenant columns, and added an analyze step after large backfills with query-plan regression monitoring.
outcome: Commit validation recorded report runtime falling from 184s to 19s and temporary writes from 6GB to 140MB; the largest tenant still took 43s.
applicable_when: Queries degrade immediately after bulk data changes and estimated row counts diverge from actual counts; useful across reporting and pipeline repositories.

title: Worker memory leak from retained delivery listeners
problem: The Messaging team found Node.js email workers restarting every four hours even with stable throughput.
symptoms: RSS rose from 220MB to the 1GB container limit; heap snapshots showed DeliveryTracker objects retained by EventEmitter listeners and logs contained MaxListenersExceededWarning.
root_cause: Each send registered a delivery listener but the timeout path never removed it, retaining the message payload and closure indefinitely.

attempted_solutions.solution: Raised the container memory limit to 2GB.
attempted_solutions.result: Restarts moved to roughly eight hours, confirming that the retained object growth continued.

successful_solution: Removed listeners in a finally block on success, timeout, and cancellation, and bounded the number of in-flight deliveries.
outcome: PR soak-test evidence showed RSS between 230MB and 310MB for 24 hours at 200 messages/sec, with no OOM restarts; normal GC pauses remained.
applicable_when: Memory grows monotonically with completed work and heap retainers point to listeners or callbacks; applicable to event-driven API and job workers.

title: CPU spikes from repeated route-pattern compilation
problem: The Web Experience team saw the server-rendered storefront slow dramatically after introducing tenant-specific redirects.
symptoms: Node CPU hit one full core per process at 120 requests/sec; SSR p95 rose from 180ms to 1.9s while network and database spans stayed short. Profiles attributed 68% of CPU to RegExp construction.
root_cause: The redirect middleware compiled all 4,000 tenant route patterns on every request instead of reusing compiled patterns.

attempted_solutions.solution: Added response compression tuning.
attempted_solutions.result: CPU profiles and p95 were unchanged because regex compilation dominated before rendering.

successful_solution: Compiled redirect patterns once per configuration version and stored them in a size-bounded tenant cache invalidated on configuration changes.
outcome: Issue replay reduced SSR p95 from 1.9s to 260ms and CPU per request by 61%; cold tenant configuration loads still took about 500ms.
applicable_when: CPU-bound request latency with healthy downstream services and repeated parsing or compilation in profiles; useful for gateway routing and policy engines.

title: Kafka lag grows because enrichment blocks the poll loop
problem: The Data Engineering team saw shipment enrichment fall 40 minutes behind during a supplier API slowdown.
symptoms: Consumer lag reached 1.8 million records, poll intervals exceeded max.poll.interval.ms, and repeated partition revocations appeared while enrichment calls took 3-6s each.
root_cause: Synchronous HTTP enrichment inside the Kafka poll loop prevented timely polling and triggered rebalances, repeatedly discarding unfinished batches.

attempted_solutions.solution: Raised max.poll.interval.ms to 15 minutes.
attempted_solutions.result: Rebalances became less frequent but throughput stayed below ingestion, so lag kept growing.

successful_solution: Decoupled polling from bounded enrichment workers, paused partitions under backpressure, preserved per-partition completion order, and committed only contiguous completed offsets.
outcome: PR replay drained 1.8 million records in 52 minutes with no poll-timeout rebalances; steady-state lag stayed below 8,000 records during a four-hour test.
applicable_when: Kafka lag accompanies slow per-record I/O and poll-timeout rebalances; applicable to notification and analytics consumers.

title: Duplicate settlement events credit the ledger twice
problem: The Ledger team found 37 duplicate credits after a settlement consumer restarted during broker maintenance.
symptoms: Two ledger rows shared each provider_event_id, and logs showed a crash after transaction commit but before the Kafka offset commit.
root_cause: At-least-once delivery replayed committed events, and the consumer had no durable deduplication inside the ledger transaction.

attempted_solutions.solution: Enabled Kafka producer idempotence.
attempted_solutions.result: Replayed consumer records still created duplicate ledger rows; producer deduplication did not cover database side effects.

successful_solution: Added a unique (provider, provider_event_id) receipt written in the same transaction as the credit, treated conflicts as already processed, and reconciled the 37 historical duplicates.
outcome: Issue evidence included a 100,000-event replay with injected crashes that produced zero additional credits; reconciliation accounted for all 37 duplicate postings.
applicable_when: An event can be redelivered after a database commit; relevant to checkout, notification, and pipeline consumers performing durable side effects.

title: Rolling deployments fail during slow application startup
problem: The Runtime team could not roll out a new JVM order worker image without repeated pod restarts.
symptoms: Pods restarted at 30s with liveness probe failures, but local startup required 65-80s to load validation rules; rollout progress deadlines expired.
root_cause: Liveness probes started before legitimate initialization finished, killing otherwise healthy containers before they could become ready.

attempted_solutions.solution: Increased the deployment progress deadline to 20 minutes.
attempted_solutions.result: Pods still restarted every 30s, so the rollout simply failed later.

successful_solution: Added a startup probe allowing up to 120s, kept readiness false until initialization completed, and retained a short liveness threshold after startup.
outcome: PR rollout logs showed 12 consecutive successful deployments with zero startup restarts; rollout duration remained about three minutes.
applicable_when: Containers are killed at a repeatable interval during initialization and eventually start outside Kubernetes; transferable to any service with expensive startup.

title: CI install fails because Node versions differ
problem: The Developer Experience team saw clean frontend builds fail only on the shared CI runner after a package upgrade.
symptoms: npm ci exited with EBADENGINE: a build dependency required Node >=20 while CI used Node 18. Local machines on Node 20 built successfully.
root_cause: The repository declared no enforced runtime version and the CI image tag still resolved to the older major version.

attempted_solutions.solution: Deleted the npm download cache and reran the workflow.
attempted_solutions.result: The engine error reproduced before compilation because cached packages were not the cause.

successful_solution: Pinned Node 20.11.1 in CI and the local version file, declared the supported engine range, and added an early runtime-version check to the build script.
outcome: Commit checks showed 20 consecutive clean installs passing on fresh runners; the early check produced a clear error on the old runtime.
applicable_when: CI-only dependency failures correlate with runtime versions rather than source changes; useful for frontend and Node-based service repositories.

title: Valid JWTs rejected after signing-key rotation
problem: The Identity team rotated the token signing key and observed intermittent 401s from internal APIs for newly issued tokens.
symptoms: 401s affected 18% of requests; failing pods logged unknown kid while tokens validated on newly restarted pods. Their JWKS caches were 24 hours old.
root_cause: Verifiers only refreshed JWKS on the daily timer and never refreshed on an unknown key ID, so long-lived pods could not recognize the new key.

attempted_solutions.solution: Extended token expiration from 15 to 60 minutes.
attempted_solutions.result: New tokens still used the unrecognized signing key, so the rejection rate did not improve.

successful_solution: Added a rate-limited refresh-on-unknown-kid path with single-flight fetching, shortened cache refresh to five minutes, and retained old public keys through the token validity window.
outcome: Issue rotation rehearsal showed unknown-kid failures below 0.05%, resolved within five seconds; expired or invalid signatures continued to be rejected.
applicable_when: Authentication failures depend on pod age or key rotation and log unknown key IDs; applicable to all services validating shared issuer tokens.

title: Concurrent purchases oversell the last inventory unit
problem: The Commerce team accepted two orders for the final unit of a limited-edition product during a flash sale.
symptoms: Race replay produced 11 oversells in 10,000 paired requests; each transaction read stock=1 before independently decrementing it.
root_cause: The availability check and decrement were separate operations without row locking or an atomic conditional update.

attempted_solutions.solution: Disabled the frontend purchase button after the first click.
attempted_solutions.result: Requests from separate shoppers still raced, so client-side prevention did not enforce inventory consistency.

successful_solution: Replaced read-then-write with UPDATE inventory SET stock=stock-1 WHERE sku=? AND stock>0, required one affected row, and recorded the reservation in the same transaction with a unique order key.
outcome: PR concurrency run accepted exactly one reservation for the last unit across 50,000 races; duplicate order retries returned the original reservation.
applicable_when: A shared counter or quota is checked before a separate write; transferable to payments limits and notification quotas.

title: Ledger transfers deadlock when accounts are locked in opposite order
problem: The Ledger team saw transfer failures rise when customers moved balances between the same pairs of accounts.
symptoms: PostgreSQL reported 40P01 on 2.3% of transfers; deadlock graphs showed one transaction holding account A and waiting for B while another held B and waited for A.
root_cause: Transactions locked the sender first and recipient second, creating opposing lock orders for reverse-direction transfers.

attempted_solutions.solution: Raised lock_timeout from 1s to 10s.
attempted_solutions.result: PostgreSQL still detected the lock cycle and aborted a participant; longer waiting could not resolve the ordering bug.

successful_solution: Locked both account rows in ascending account ID order across all transfer paths and retried deadlock-aborted transactions with bounded jitter and the original idempotency key.
outcome: Commit stress results reduced deadlock failures from 2.3% to below 0.01% across one million bidirectional transfers; contention still raised hot-account p95 to 620ms.
applicable_when: Deadlock graphs show transactions acquiring the same resources in different orders; useful for inventory reservations and multi-entity updates.

title: Background jobs remain stuck after worker termination
problem: The Messaging team found scheduled SMS jobs permanently marked running after a node drain.
symptoms: About 1,400 jobs were older than two hours although normal execution took under 10s; their owner pod IDs no longer existed and queue depth appeared normal.
root_cause: The PostgreSQL-backed job runner changed status to running without a lease expiry or recovery path for crashed workers.

attempted_solutions.solution: Scaled the worker deployment from 4 to 12 pods.
attempted_solutions.result: New workers selected only pending jobs, leaving orphaned running jobs untouched.

successful_solution: Added expiring leases with heartbeats and fencing tokens, reclaimed expired jobs, and used the job ID as the SMS provider idempotency key to make uncertain sends safe to retry.
outcome: Issue recovery audit reclaimed all 1,400 jobs in 18 minutes; a subsequent termination drill recovered work within 90s with no duplicate provider sends.
applicable_when: Jobs remain running after their workers disappear; useful for any durable queue with application-managed ownership.

title: Partner API ingestion stalls on rate-limit responses
problem: The Integrations team doubled ingestion workers and saw account synchronization take longer instead of finishing sooner.
symptoms: Partner responses were 62% HTTP 429, Retry-After was usually 30s, and synchronization p95 rose from 8 to 47 minutes.
root_cause: Each worker independently assumed it could use the entire account-level request quota and retried immediately after a 429.

attempted_solutions.solution: Added four more workers to clear the backlog.
attempted_solutions.result: The shared quota was exceeded more often and useful throughput fell another 20%.

successful_solution: Introduced a shared per-account token bucket, honored Retry-After, used jittered backoff, and scheduled accounts fairly so a large tenant could not consume every slot.
outcome: PR partner-response logs showed 429s falling to 1.8% and sync p95 to 11 minutes; large initial imports still required several quota windows.
applicable_when: More parallelism reduces throughput against a shared external quota; relevant to email, payment-provider, and data-import clients.

title: Profile cache resurrects old data after an update
problem: The Identity team received reports that saved display names briefly reverted across devices.
symptoms: Roughly 0.7% of profile edits returned the old value for up to ten minutes. Traces showed a slow reader filling Redis immediately after the writer deleted the cache key.
root_cause: A reader fetched the old database row before the update committed, then repopulated the invalidated cache afterward; deletion alone did not order concurrent fills.

attempted_solutions.solution: Reduced the cache TTL from ten minutes to one minute.
attempted_solutions.result: The stale interval shrank, but the race still occurred and database read load increased.

successful_solution: Included a monotonic profile version in cache values and used an atomic Redis script to reject older fills; committed updates emitted durable outbox invalidations that advanced a version watermark.
outcome: Issue race test rejected every delayed old-version fill in 50,000 schedules; production stale-read reports fell below 0.02%, with outbox delay still allowing brief staleness.
applicable_when: Cache values revert after successful writes because in-flight reads refill old state; useful for catalog and notification preference caches.

title: Schema migration blocks writes on a large events table
problem: The Data Engineering team deployed an events-column type change during active ingestion and blocked writers for nine minutes.
symptoms: Insert p95 exceeded 30s, pg_locks showed an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, and a table rewrite was running on 480GB of historical events.
root_cause: The migration changed text to jsonb in place, requiring a long rewrite while holding a lock incompatible with ingestion.

attempted_solutions.solution: Increased the migration statement timeout to one hour.
attempted_solutions.result: The operation could run longer, but it continued blocking writes and exceeded the ingestion availability budget.

successful_solution: Cancelled and rolled back the blocking migration, added a nullable jsonb column with a short lock timeout, dual-wrote new events, backfilled in throttled batches, and switched reads after validating counts and conversion errors.
outcome: PR migration log showed backfill finishing in 31 hours with insert p95 below 180ms; 0.04% invalid JSON rows were quarantined for correction before retiring the old column.
applicable_when: A schema change rewrites a large active table or needs a prolonged exclusive lock; transferable to payments and user data migrations.

title: Indexer containers crash on oversized bulk batches
problem: The Discovery team saw indexer pods crash whenever a nightly catalog import contained unusually large product descriptions.
symptoms: Pods ended with OOMKilled and exit code 137 during bulk serialization; RSS jumped from 350MB to 1.5GB in seconds, then reset after restart.
root_cause: The batcher capped document count at 5,000 but not bytes, and simultaneously retained object payloads and the serialized HTTP request body.

attempted_solutions.solution: Forced garbage collection between batches.
attempted_solutions.result: The oversized live batch still exceeded the container limit before it could be sent or collected.

successful_solution: Capped batches by encoded bytes and document count, limited concurrent bulk requests to two, and routed individually oversized documents to an explicit rejection queue.
outcome: Issue replay indexed the full import with peak RSS of 620MB under a 1GB limit; 19 oversized documents required manual content cleanup.
applicable_when: Memory jumps during a specific large batch rather than growing across many completed batches; relevant to exports and notification bulk sends.

title: Dependency upgrade breaks password verification at startup
problem: The Identity team upgraded the Python dependency lock and found login workers failing before serving traffic.
symptoms: Containers logged AttributeError referencing a removed bcrypt module attribute when the password adapter initialized; the previous lockfile image started successfully.
root_cause: The legacy password adapter depended on an internal bcrypt attribute removed by the newly resolved version, despite permissive dependency constraints.

attempted_solutions.solution: Rebuilt the image without Docker layer caching.
attempted_solutions.result: The same locked versions reproduced the failure, ruling out stale build layers.

successful_solution: Restored the last compatible bcrypt pin as an immediate recovery, then replaced the adapter with a maintained integration and verified existing hash fixtures before upgrading again.
outcome: Commit checks verified 2,000 representative existing password hashes and new-hash round trips; the canary served login traffic for 24 hours without adapter exceptions.
applicable_when: A dependency update breaks initialization or runtime integration despite passing installation; useful for backend SDK and framework upgrades.

title: Checkout UI rejects a valid changed API response
problem: The Web Experience team deployed a backend checkout response update and saw successful orders displayed as failures.
symptoms: The API returned 201, but 7% of browser sessions logged Cannot read properties of undefined reading amount; only clients expecting total.amount were affected.
root_cause: The backend replaced the nested total object with total_minor without a compatibility period, while old JavaScript bundles remained cached on client devices.

attempted_solutions.solution: Purged the CDN JavaScript cache.
attempted_solutions.result: Already open tabs and cached service-worker bundles still used the old contract, so errors continued.

successful_solution: Restored total alongside total_minor, deployed a client that accepted both forms, added consumer contract fixtures, and removed the old field only after supported client telemetry showed migration complete.
outcome: PR browser replay passed for old and new bundles; checkout rendering errors fell from 7% to 0.1% while successful order creation remained unchanged.
applicable_when: HTTP success is followed by client parse or rendering errors after a schema change; applicable to mobile and service-to-service consumers with independent deployments.

title: Missing trace propagation hides the source of intermittent latency
problem: The Runtime team spent two incidents guessing why order submission occasionally took three seconds across checkout, auth, and shipping services.
symptoms: Aggregate endpoint metrics showed p99 of 3.2s, but logs had unrelated request IDs and traces ended at the checkout boundary; no downstream timing could be attributed to the slow requests.
root_cause: The HTTP client wrapper dropped traceparent headers and instrumentation excluded outbound requests, leaving a diagnostic gap rather than evidence of a specific performance cause.

attempted_solutions.solution: Enabled debug logging on every service.
attempted_solutions.result: Log volume tripled without shared correlation IDs, so engineers still could not reconstruct an individual slow request.

successful_solution: Instrumented inbound and outbound HTTP, propagated W3C trace context through the client wrapper, attached trace IDs to structured logs, and retained slow traces with collector tail sampling.
outcome: Reviewed incident-drill notes showed time to isolate a delayed shipping hop dropping from 75 to 12 minutes; p99 remained 3.2s because instrumentation itself did not fix latency.
applicable_when: Latency crosses service boundaries but evidence cannot identify the responsible hop; useful before selecting a database, cache, or downstream-service fix.

title: Nested retries amplify a brief webhook outage
problem: The Messaging team experienced a 15-minute backlog after a customer webhook endpoint failed for only 90 seconds.
symptoms: Outbound attempts rose from 300 to 3,600/sec, worker utilization hit 100%, and the same delivery IDs appeared repeatedly in HTTP and queue retry logs.
root_cause: The HTTP SDK retried three times inside each of four queue delivery attempts, multiplying retries without a shared attempt budget or jitter.

attempted_solutions.solution: Raised the worker concurrency from 50 to 200.
attempted_solutions.result: More duplicate attempts reached the failing endpoint and the backlog expanded faster.

successful_solution: Made the queue the sole retry owner, disabled SDK retries, added exponential backoff with full jitter and a per-destination circuit breaker, and preserved delivery idempotency keys.
outcome: Issue outage replay capped attempts at 480/sec and drained the backlog four minutes after recovery; 0.3% of deliveries exhausted the budget and entered the dead-letter queue.
applicable_when: A short dependency failure causes traffic amplification and prolonged recovery through nested retries; transferable to payment and ingestion clients.

title: Service-to-service TLS fails after certificate renewal
problem: The Commerce team lost shipping quotes immediately after the internal shipping endpoint renewed its certificate.
symptoms: Quote calls returned 502 on 100% of checkout pods with x509: certificate signed by unknown authority; curl using the platform trust bundle succeeded and database metrics were normal.
root_cause: The checkout image embedded an outdated private CA bundle, while the renewed shipping certificate chained to the new intermediate trusted by the platform bundle.

attempted_solutions.solution: Restarted checkout pods and flushed DNS.
attempted_solutions.result: New pods loaded the same outdated image bundle and failed the same TLS handshake.

successful_solution: Mounted the managed CA bundle into checkout, configured the HTTP client to use it, rebuilt pooled connections on bundle rotation, and added a staging handshake check for the next certificate chain.
outcome: Reviewed rotation notes recorded shipping quote success returning to 99.8% within eight minutes; a second certificate rotation completed without trust failures.
applicable_when: Internal calls fail during TLS negotiation after certificate rotation while DNS and service health remain good; relevant to every private-CA service client.
